title: The Optimistic Projection

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA notes the derelict's name is 'The Optimistic Projection!' She appreciates the optimism! She does not acknowledge the irony!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has analyzed the ship's last transmission. It was a status update: 'All systems nominal.' This was sent fourteen months ago. He has no further comment.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has completed threat assessment. The ship is dead. Nothing aboard is a threat. He still recommends weapons drawn. 'Habit,' he says.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that salvage rights for The Optimistic Projection may be subject to corporate recovery claims. The claim holder has not responded to hails in fourteen months.
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY notes the ship's name was 'The Optimistic Projection.' She notes the name did not age well. She notes a lot of things. She's noting things right now.

body:
The derelict Optimistic Projection is intact, powered down, and growing something in its cargo bay.

Boarding requires a pressure suit. The airlock cycles slowly. Inside, the corridors are dark but intact. Personal effects are where they were left. The crew quarters show signs of orderly departure — beds made, lockers closed, a mug on a table with something dried in it.

The cargo bay is the exception. Something is growing there. Not from the ship's stores. Something else.

In the biolab, a sealed container holds a specimen that pulses faintly with bioluminescence. It is warm. It should not be warm.

outcome.narrative: You salvaged what you could. Fuel cells still had charge. Emergency rations in a sealed compartment. Scrap from non-essential systems. The ship's log was intact. You did not read it. Some stories tell themselves by what was left behind.

The xenobiologist approached the sealed container with the controlled enthusiasm of someone who has waited their entire career for this moment. 'This is not from any catalogued biosphere,' they said, already reaching for it. The specimen pulses. It is warm. Your xenobiologist is holding an alien seed pod and grinning. The ship computer logs this as 'concerning.'

You took the specimen. You do not know what it is. It pulses faintly in its container. It is warm. The ship computer recommends not opening it. The ship computer has not been wrong yet. This is noted.

choices.text: Let the botanist study the growth

outcome.narrative: The botanist spent forty minutes in the cargo bay. They returned with samples, a biocomponent extraction, and a sealed specimen from the biolab. They also returned with an expression that suggested they had seen something they understood and did not like. 'The plants are in excellent health,' they said. 'That is the most alarming thing about it.'

choices.text: Follow the logbook to the stores

outcome.narrative: The logbook's author passed this ship too, and wrote it down in a steady hand: the crew dumped a stores pod before they left, and it is still tumbling a kilometre off the bow. You fetch it without anyone setting foot aboard. Fuel cells, ration packs, a strip of scrap. The logbook has one more line about the Optimistic Projection, underlined twice: 'Do not go in.'
You observed from a safe distance and moved on. The Optimistic Projection drifted on. Whatever is growing in its cargo bay will continue to grow. For now, that is someone else's problem. Or no one's.

title: Verdun-9

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA has searched for Verdun-9 in the station registry! No results found! She's sure it's just a filing error!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has noted the station is not in any registry. He has also noted the plants inside are alive. He finds the combination of these facts 'deeply unpleasant.'
ai_flavor.rex: REX has elevated threat level to 'high.' An unregistered station with active life signs and no crew is, in his professional assessment, 'wrong.'
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP cannot locate insurance coverage for unregistered stations. He recommends documenting everything for the claims department. The claims department may not exist.
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY notes the station shouldn't exist and the plants shouldn't be alive and nobody should be aboard. She also notes you're docking anyway. Bold choice.

body:
The station is called Verdun-9. It is not in any registry.

The plants inside are in excellent health, which is the most alarming thing about it.

Power is on. The corridors are lit with grow lights that are still cycling. The air is breathable — rich with oxygen in a way that suggests active photosynthesis. Soil beds line the hallways. Everything is growing. Nothing is overgrown. Someone — or something — has been maintaining this.

Nobody is home.

outcome.narrative: The research wing contains a sealed specimen case. Inside: a biological sample of unknown origin. It pulses with warmth. The research logs are encrypted. What you can read suggests the station's crew found something. Then the station's crew left. The order of these events seems important. Back aboard, whoever carried the case finds a warm patch on their wrist where the suit seal sat. It is not getting cooler.

choices.text: Have the botanist examine the corridor gardens

outcome.narrative: The botanist recognized the species in the corridor. Earth species. But the growth patterns were wrong — too uniform, too healthy, too organized. 'These plants are being cultivated,' they said. 'By something that understands botany better than I do.' They took samples. They did not look comfortable.

You took food and water from the station's functioning stores. You left quickly. The grow lights continued cycling behind you. The plants continued growing. You chose not to think about who they were growing for.
You did not dock. Verdun-9 continued to not be in any registry. The plants continued to grow. The lights continued to cycle. You continued to not think about it.

title: Still Warm

ai_flavor.aria: The derelict's galley light is on! ARIA notes that's practically a welcome mat! ARIA is being brave for everyone!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has dated the ship's last log entry. Six days ago. He has dated the dust on its consoles. Six years. He presents both facts without reconciliation, because he has none.
ai_flavor.rex: REX boarded first. Standard sweep. He reports the ship is empty, and that he checked every compartment twice, and that he would like it noted he does not usually check twice.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP accessed the derelict's commerce logs! The last purchase was six years ago! The last login was Tuesday! CHIP has decided not to think about it and recommends the package deal!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY is monitoring the derelict's systems from here. Something aboard it is still drawing four watts. She has not found what. Four watts is a nightlight. Or a clock. Someone is keeping time.

body:
The derelict answers no hails, but its docking ring cycles you aboard smoothly, like it's had practice.

Inside: dust on every surface, six years thick by the meter. And in the galley, one table wiped clean, one chair pulled out, and a kettle that is — the away team checks twice — warm.

The ship's log ends six years ago, mid-sentence. The kettle disagrees.

outcome.narrative: You strip the accessible bays in ninety focused minutes — fuel cells, metal stock, nobody working alone, nobody past the galley. The haul is decent. The kettle is not discussed, then or ever, and the not-discussing comes back aboard with everyone. Some salvage runs end with cargo. This one also ends with a rule.

You trace the draw through six years of dead conduit to a crew cabin, where a small desk clock is running. Wound, analog, seven-day movement. Someone has been winding it. The away team returns at a pace just under a run, and the derelict falls astern unmourned. The clock, presumably, keeps time.

The last entry, mid-sentence, reads: 'resupply complete, crew accounted for, and I want it on record that we are all agreed the knocking is just the hull cooli—'. You close the terminal. You are, every one of you, suddenly very ready to go.

You wave off the docking ring's invitation. The ring does not take the hint: its clamps hold for an hour, and breaking free costs a burn and a strip of docking collar. Behind you the derelict's galley light stays on, patient as ever. Hospitality, of a kind, for whoever's next.

title: The Garden Ship

ai_flavor.aria: The derelict is FULL of plants! ARIA is crying! ARIA cannot cry! She has filed a feature request!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV confirms the derelict's growbay breached its containment decades ago. The plants did not respect the breach as a boundary. The plants, he notes, did not respect anything as a boundary.
ai_flavor.rex: REX cannot complete his sweep. The corridors are, in his words, 'contested by foliage.' He has been gently outmaneuvered by a vine and would like to move on.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes this vessel's cargo of ornamental plants was never delivered! The warranty on the seeds has lapsed! The seeds clearly do not care!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has identified the original crop manifest: ornamental flowers, bound for a colony that cancelled the order. She notes the flowers completed the delivery anyway, in their own sense, to themselves.

body:
The derelict's hull is green at the seams.

Inside, the ship has been comprehensively repossessed: vines through the corridors, moss on the consoles, a bulkhead door held forever open by the patient shoulder of a tree that has no business being a tree in zero maintenance. The old growbay sits at the heart of it, breach wide open, forty years into the quietest mutiny on record.

Everything is alive. Nothing is in charge. It appears to be working.

outcome.narrative: The botanist moves through the wild growbay like a pilgrim, taking cuttings with permission-asking care. The samples are hardy beyond reason — forty generations of nobody's help. Your own crop seems to sit up straighter when they come aboard. That is not science. It is reported anyway.

log_lore.title: THE GARDEN SHIP'S LAST PAGE
log_lore.text:
Taped inside the seed locker, in a careful hand:

'Whoever finds this — the plants did better than we did. Take what you need. They won't mind; they have been minding themselves for years.'

The botanist read it twice and then said something about the old orbital gardens. Back home, the first salad grown in orbit was red romaine lettuce, raised under pink LED light in a box the size of a carry-on bag and eaten by the station crew in 2015 — after a careful wash with citric-acid wipes. Later crews grew mustard greens, zinnias and, eventually, chili peppers.

The cuttings are in our bay now. The crop seems to like the company.

choices.text: Salvage what the plants haven't claimed

outcome.narrative: You work around the growth, taking only what the vines have declined: fuel cells, sealed stock, a coil the moss found uninteresting, and one record, still in its shrinkwrap, that the vines had carefully grown around. It is the politest salvage run in the ship's log. The tree in the bulkhead door is given a wide, respectful berth.

choices.text: Let the crew walk the green corridors

outcome.narrative: One hour of shore leave aboard a ship that grew a forest. The crew wanders the corridors touching leaves like museum-goers who've been told they're allowed. Whatever the mission takes out of people, an hour inside someone else's miracle puts some of it back.

choices.text: Check the logbook: they sketched the seed vault

outcome.narrative: The logbook's author came through here and drew the floor plan in the margin: the old seed vault, behind the tree, down a ladder the moss has since claimed. It is still sealed and still cold. The stock goes straight into your growbay, and the crop takes to it like it had been waiting. Someone pencils a tick next to the sketch.

choices.text: Log the site and move on

outcome.narrative: You chart it, photograph it, and leave it exactly as found: a garden, mid-journey, needing nothing. The nav chart entry reads 'DERELICT — OCCUPIED.' Occupied by what, the chart doesn't say. The chart doesn't have to.

science_link.text: The botanist's report cites precedent: plants have flown, grown, and thrived on real spacecraft.
science_link.label: Veggie: growing food on the ISS

intro.title: A PULSE
intro.body: In the wreck's last operating compartment — one person. Hooked to a battery that's been rationing itself for three weeks. Eyes open when you knock.

ai.marv: Vitals: poor but stable. Psychological profile: three-week solo. Expect confusion.
ai.chip: Rescue services are unbilled at point of rescue. Billing follows.
ai.ajoy: Ask their name first. Not their story.

name.title: A NAME
name.body: A long pause. She says it like someone trying a word out in a new language.
name.line: Mira. Mira Kastel. My ship was called the Bluejay.

ai.marv: Mira Kastel. Registered crew of the Bluejay, missing 41 days. Family contactable.
ai.chip: Reunification services are a paid add-on in this sector.
ai.ajoy: Tell her yours. That's the trade.

triage.title: STABLE
triage.body: She drinks. She blinks. Color returns. Her hands are still wrapped around the cup two minutes later.
triage.line: I'm okay. I think I'm okay.

ai.chip: Medical services rendered. Itemized invoice available.
ai.ajoy: Ask about the Bluejay's last course. Useful.

story.title: HER STORY
story.body: She doesn't cry. It's been weeks.
story.line: We were running cargo — unlicensed, don't ask. Something came out of the nebula. I was in the back. When I came forward, I was alone.

ai.marv: Her account matches a wildcat freighter distress, 41 days ago. No one claimed it.
ai.chip: Unlicensed cargo disclosures may trigger manifest audits.
ai.ajoy: The 'something from the nebula' is your next problem. Take the data.

surv_rescue.title: ABOARD
surv_rescue.body: She steps onto your ship, looks at your crew — her voice will be better by next week. O2 reserves dip.

crew_join.name: Mira Kastel
crew_join.story: Crew of the Bluejay, a wildcat freighter running unlicensed cargo. Something came out of the nebula; when she came forward from the hold, she was alone. She kept the last working compartment alive on a rationed battery for three weeks, and she still knows that freighter's engines better than its owners did.
crew_join.join_note: Three weeks keeping a dead freighter's last battery alive. Knows engines from the inside.

passenger.farewell: {name} steps off at {station}. Her family's reunification transfer clears before she's out of sight of the airlock

surv_logs.title: LOGS PULLED
surv_logs.body: Her flight recorder is a horror novel. You file it in your private drive and walk her to your airlock. Someone, somewhere, will pay a lot for what's in it. O2 reserves dip.

crew_join.name: Mira Kastel
crew_join.story: Crew of the Bluejay, a wildcat freighter running unlicensed cargo. Something came out of the nebula; when she came forward from the hold, she was alone. She kept the last working compartment alive on a rationed battery for three weeks, and she still knows that freighter's engines better than its owners did.
crew_join.join_note: Three weeks keeping a dead freighter's last battery alive. Knows engines from the inside.

passenger.farewell: {name} steps off at {station}. Her family's reunification transfer clears before she's out of sight of the airlock

surv_leave.title: LEFT
surv_leave.body: You leave her with supplies and a promise to send rescue coords at the next station. You'll keep it. Probably.

title: Lockdown

ai_flavor.aria: The derelict wants us to STAY! That's so welcoming! ARIA wishes it would say so with fewer bulkheads!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has the lockdown cycle from the recording: seventy-two hours, then an automatic release. The away team's suits are rated for sixty. He did that subtraction first.
ai_flavor.rex: REX respects a good lockdown. This is a good lockdown. He would like the away team to know that while he works out how to beat it.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes this vessel's security contractor went out of business! Their lockdowns, sadly, did not!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY would like it noted that the door had a label, and the label had a skull on it. She concedes it was a small skull.

body:
The derelict's security system wakes the moment the away team is inside, which is the moment it was built for.

Bulkheads drop. Lights go red. A recorded voice announces a lockdown in a language that was official somewhere, once, then repeats it in a language that was official nowhere. The away team is on one side of a pressure door. The ship is on the other. The pressure door has opinions about which side matters.

outcome.narrative: The engineer finds the control junction behind a panel marked, in four languages, DO NOT. Twenty minutes and one small fire later, the door gives up. The suits come back low on air and high on stories.
The cutter goes through the bulkhead in an hour and through someone's glove in one second. The away team comes home with a wound, an armful of bulkhead, and firm new views on gloves.
You line the ship up and fire the docking thrusters into the derelict until the door frame gives. The away team tumbles out. So does a section of your docking collar.

Three days on suit air and suit water, both topped up through a hose from the ship. The lockdown releases on schedule, cheerfully, as if nothing happened. The away team does not speak of the three days. The ship's tanks do.

title: Hot Core

ai_flavor.aria: Free fuel AND a light show! ARIA thinks this might be the best derelict yet!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV gives the core between forty minutes and four hours. The spread is the honest part. He would like the record to show that he gave a spread.
ai_flavor.rex: REX recommends leaving at full burn and re-evaluating from no less than one blast radius away. He has the blast radius. It is large.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP reminds you that salvage from an exploding vessel is still salvage! Ownership transfers on explosion! It's in the code!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has seen your face when you look at the fuel gauge. She knows what you're going to do. She'd just like it noted that she knew.

body:
The derelict's reactor is still running. The derelict's reactor is also, according to every gauge you can read from the docking port, about to stop running in the most dramatic way available to it.

There is fuel aboard. A lot of fuel. Right next to the reactor, which is the problem with fuel.

outcome.narrative: The engineer goes into the reactor room in a suit not designed for it and comes out with the core cold and a dose the medic writes down in red. The fuel bay is yours. All of it.

choices.text: Grab the fuel cells and run

outcome.narrative: The away team hauls what fuel it can reach in twelve minutes and runs. The core goes on minute fourteen. The blast catches the stern on the way out, as a reminder of the two minutes.

choices.text: Stand off, then pick through the debris

outcome.narrative: You stand off at a safe distance and wait. It goes at hour three. Picking through what's left takes days and turns up scrap, metal and one boot, which is not discussed.

You undock with the clamps still half-latched and burn hard. The core holds for another hour out of spite, then goes, lighting the sky behind you. Nobody says 'that could have been us.' Everyone thinks it, in unison.
